segments.text: Think back about 25 years.
If you made a spreadsheet, you probably saved it directly to your computer's hard drive.
If that drive crashed and you forgot to make a backup, your work was gone.
Today, using something like Google Sheets, you can just close your laptop,
pull up the exact same file on your phone, and pick up right where you left off.
That seamless handoff is what we call the cloud.
It is simply a network of remote computers that you access over the Internet
to store files and run programs.
Our frictionless digital life completely depends on this invisible remote hardware
quietly keeping a copy of everything we do.
Now, instead of just saving that spreadsheet, imagine you share it with chat GPT
and ask, why did my expenses jump in March?
Storing a file is a simple job, but writing a response takes significantly more computing power
because an AI model constructs its answers entirely out of math.
Every single word the AI reads or writes is represented by a vector,
a row of thousands of numbers.
As those numbers pass through the model's layers,
they are constantly updated to account for the context of the words around them.
This graphic breaks down how fast that math adds up.
Processing just one piece of a word, a token, takes roughly 100 billion calculations.
A short 75-word answer requires 10 trillion calculations.
A longer conversation pushes that workload to a staggering 100 trillion calculations.
Even a brief, seemingly simple text response
requires an astronomical amount of invisible math to reach your screen.
The raw ability to run all of those calculations is what the tech industry calls compute.
Those trillions of calculations are just for one question from one person.
Now, multiply that by millions of people asking their own questions
at the exact same time.
All of that simultaneous math has to physically happen somewhere.
It happens inside a data center.
A data center is a massive building filled with servers.
For AI, these servers use specialized chips called GPUs,
which are designed specifically to run many calculations at once.
These structures have a colossal footprint.
Some cover the area of several football fields
and consume as much electricity as a small city.
When you step inside one of these AI data centers,
the sheer scale of the hardware becomes clear.
Look at the person walking down that aisle on the left.
That single human figure gives you a sense of the immense
towering scale of this equipment.
Those tall cabinets, stretching upward, are server racks.
Each rack holds multiple individual servers,
tightly stacked one on top of another.
Following that aisle toward the far wall,
you pass seemingly endless rows of these racks.
The digital cloud is made entirely of this massive, heavy machinery
grinding away around the clock.
With a footprint that massive,
we have to look outside the building and ask what this means
for the people living nearby.
This outlines four local impacts.
Upper left.
Data centers could use 12% of U.S. electricity by 2030,
raising bills.
Upper right.
Cooling chips takes a million gallons of fresh water on hot days.
Bottom left.
Constant cooling fan noise causes lost sleep.
Bottom right.
While many build it, few permanent jobs remain.
The global demand for artificial intelligence relies entirely
on the local resources of the towns that host these machines.
AI companies are working to address these pressures.
They are securing more electricity for the grid,
implementing better water recycling,
and developing newer chips that can do the same math with less power.
This brings us to a stark reality captured in this brief text.
Behind the immediate answer on your screen is a massive data center.
And for someone else,
that massive data center is just a part of their daily neighborhood.
The weightless invisible cloud is an illusion.
It is built out of heavy metal, immense power,
and millions of gallons of water firmly rooted in our physical world.
